vignette:
He is twenty-six, a European man who has spent most of his life on the water. Before the trauma, he works as a fisherman the way his father does: waking in the dark, pulling on damp wool layers, heading out before sunrise with a crew that knows one another mostly through routine and weather. He marries young, and in his telling those first years feel plain and solid in a way he now misses. He remembers salt on his hands, the ache in his shoulders after hauling nets, coming home tired enough to sleep without effort. He says there was a time when his body belonged to him without question.

The change begins on a voyage that is supposed to be ordinary. Their boat is operating near disputed waters, and he recalls first noticing another vessel only as a shape moving too fast toward them. Men board carrying weapons, shouting in a language he only partly understands. He and the others are forced to the deck, hands bound behind their backs with rough cord that bites into his wrists. At first he thinks it is a robbery or some kind of detention that will pass if he keeps still and does what he is told. Instead, he is taken ashore with two crewmen and held in a concrete room without windows.

When he speaks about what happens there, he does so in fragments, as if the story breaks apart when it gets too close. He remembers being stripped and beaten when he cannot answer questions to their satisfaction. He remembers water thrown over him, long stretches of standing with his arms restrained until his shoulders feel as if they are tearing, blows to his ribs and thighs, a boot against the side of his face. More than the pain, he remembers the humiliation: men watching him, laughing, deciding when he can sit, drink, use a toilet. He says the worst part is not always knowing when they will come back through the door. Time becomes unreal. He tries to count, to pray, to picture his wife hanging laundry in the yard, but eventually even those images begin to blur. What stays sharp is the feeling that he has become an object in someone else's hands.

He is released after several days through an arrangement he still does not fully understand. By then he is dehydrated, bruised, and moving stiffly. His wife meets him when he returns, and he can see her trying not to stare at his face. He tells her almost nothing. He says he is tired. He says he just needs to get back to normal. In the first weeks he insists on returning to the harbor, but the ordinary sounds of work have changed. The slam of metal against the deck makes his whole body jerk. A shout from another boat sends him turning before he knows why. He scans the horizon constantly, unable to stop himself. Other men joke that he is jumpy now, and he laughs with them, but inside he feels ashamed of how quickly fear takes over.

Sleep becomes the place he dreads most. He wakes soaked in sweat after dreams in which he is back in the room, unable to move his hands. Sometimes he comes awake swinging, once striking the wall hard enough to split the skin over his knuckles. His wife learns not to touch him suddenly at night. She lies awake listening to his breathing change, waiting to see whether he will settle or bolt upright again. In the mornings he tells her he is fine, though he is exhausted and irritable before the day has begun.

He starts avoiding anything that reminds him of the detention, though reminders seem to appear everywhere. He will not watch news about maritime conflicts. He takes a longer route to the docks to avoid a warehouse with bare concrete walls. When officials ask for a statement, he misses appointments and then says the scheduling was confused. At home, if his wife asks what he is thinking, he shrugs or leaves the room. He hates the look on her face when she sees him withdrawing, a mixture of worry and hurt that makes him feel both guilty and trapped. Before, he had been easy with affection. Now he stiffens when she reaches for his wrists.

Work, once the most familiar part of him, becomes complicated. He still goes out because fishing is what he knows and because staying home feels like surrender, but the sea no longer quiets him. He keeps noticing routes of escape, possible threats, men on distant vessels. If fog rolls in, his chest tightens. If the radio crackles with an unfamiliar voice, he feels heat rush through him. There are days he becomes so preoccupied scanning the water that he misses simple instructions, and afterward he is furious with himself. He tells himself other men have survived worse. He tells himself he should be over it by now. The harshness of that inner voice surprises him, but he cannot seem to soften it.

With his wife, he is still present in the practical ways-repairing a hinge, buying bread, remembering to pay bills-but emotionally he often feels far away, as though part of him is still shut inside that windowless room. He loves her and fears burdening her. He wants to be the man who came home tired from fishing and slept soundly beside her. Instead he lives as if danger is never fully past, measuring every room, every stranger, every sudden sound against something his body cannot forget.
